title: Accents and Pause
description: Read the accents as stress, punctuation, and chant, and recognize pausal forms.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: The accent signs of the Hebrew Bible do three jobs at once: they mark the stressed syllable of each word, they punctuate the verse, and they guide its chanting. At the main breaks of a verse a pause lengthens the stressed vowel, so a word can look different there than in the body of the verse.

blocks.caption: The three uses of the accents
blocks.html: The accents first mark the tone-syllable, guiding the pronunciation of each word; the main tone falls usually on the last syllable, though in the segholate nouns (מֶלֶךְ, king) and some verb forms it falls on the next-to-last. Second, they are signs of logical punctuation, like our commas and stops, so they are a running commentary on the sense. Third, they are musical signs, guiding the recitative by which the whole text is read. This last use embraces the other two.

blocks.caption: Pause
blocks.html: At the middle and end of a Hebrew verse a natural pause occurs, and it changes vowels. A short vowel in the tone-syllable becomes long; occasionally the tone shifts from the last syllable to the next-to-last, which is then lengthened; and a vocal shewa before the tone may rise to a full vowel. The result is that a word may appear in a different vowel-form in pause than in the body of the verse — a change to recognize, not to confuse with a different word.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not take a pausal form for a different word. מַיִם (water) appears as מָיִם at a verse break, and לַיְלָה (night) as לָיְלָה; the consonants are the same, and only the stressed vowel has lengthened.
